Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Does Treating Addiction Rebuild Lives? Evidence from Buprenorphine
Sarah Eichmeyer, Aljoscha Janssen, and Jonathan Zhang
NBER Working Paper No. 36041
November 2026
JEL No. H30, I19, I3
ABSTRACT
Does treating addiction improve economic circumstances as well as health? Using two decades of 
Veterans Health Administration records on over 140,000 patients with opioid use disorder and 
consumer credit data, we exploit staggered facility-level buprenorphine adoption and quasi-random 
emergency physician assignment. A five-percentage-point increase in the share of clinicians with 
buprenorphine prescribing experience doubles overdose survivors’ long-term medication use and 
reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 percentage points. Instrumenting receipt yields a 22 
percent credit score gain. At $300,000 per statistical life-year, estimated survival benefits alone 
exceed added medical costs within three years

1 Introduction
Does treating addiction rebuild lives? Medical innovation can generate substantial welfare
gains (Murphy and Topel, 2006; Cutler and McClellan, 2001), but whether effective treatments
also improve patients’ economic circumstances is a separate question. Addiction presents a
demanding case because illness and disadvantage are closely intertwined. First, medications
shown to be effective in controlled trials may deliver smaller benefits in routine care, where
adherence is imperfect and patients often have serious medical or psychiatric conditions that
can exclude them from trials. Second, even when treatment succeeds clinically, the poverty,
mental illness, and social isolation that accompany addiction may continue to hold down
employment and financial stability. Whether medication improves economic circumstances
despite these obstacles determines how far the benefits of expanding treatment extend beyond
health and informs the role of complementary interventions addressing those disadvantages.
These questions are especially pressing for opioid use disorder (OUD): more than 800,000
people died from opioid overdoses in the United States between 1999 and 2023 (Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention, 2025).
We quantify the health and economic returns to expanding access to buprenorphine, a
medication shown in clinical trials to improve treatment retention and reduce illicit opioid
use under controlled conditions (Mattick et al., 2014). We study its delivery in routine
care in the Veterans Health Administration, the largest integrated health system in the
United States. The setting is well-suited to the question. Eligibility for care is stable and
untied to employment, so patients can be followed with essentially no attrition. Because the
Veterans Health Administration (VA) administers social programs alongside care, we observe
health and economic life in the same administrative universe: every clinical encounter and
prescription, complete mortality, enrollment in vocational and disability programs, and, for a
subsample linked to consumer credit records, standing in the credit market. The data cover
more than 140,000 patients with OUD over two decades.
We exploit two sources of quasi-experimental variation in access to buprenorphine treat-
ment. The first is the staggered growth across facilities in the share of clinicians who prescribe
buprenorphine, which until 2023 required a federal “X-waiver” that clinicians obtained and
began using at very different times. We anchor this design on patients’ first opioid overdose
treated in a VA emergency department (ED), an objective marker of severe OUD and a
moment at which treatment is often first offered. In a difference-in-differences design with
1
patient-level panel data, we compare each patient’s change in outcomes with that of patients
who overdosed at the same facility earlier or later in its prescribing expansion, and at other
facilities at the same time, which identifies the policy effect of expanding treatment capacity.
The second is a judge leniency design applied to physicians: within a facility and quarter,
patients with OUD arriving at an ED are assigned essentially at random to physicians who
differ widely and persistently in their propensity to initiate buprenorphine, and we use this
propensity as an instrument for treatment receipt. The first design answers the policymaker’s
question, what expanding treatment capacity buys; the second answers the clinician’s, what
starting treatment does for the patient in front of them.
Wefind that expandingaccess tobuprenorphineimprovespatients’ economiccircumstances
as well as their health. The first step is treatment itself. We measure facility adoption as
the caseload-weighted share of clinicians with prior buprenorphine prescribing experience.
A five percentage point (pp) increase—roughly the gap between facilities at the 10th and
90th percentiles in 2018—raises patients’ buprenorphine use by 10 pp in the month after
an overdose. Averaged over the following two years, the increase in monthly use is 4.7 pp,
roughly doubling the pre-overdose rate. Monthly engagement with substance use disorder
treatment rises 26%.
The economic gains appear in both employment program participation and consumer
credit records. The same expansion in facility prescribing raises enrollment in VA vocational
rehabilitation and employment programs by 1.3 pp, a 65% increase from a 2% baseline.
The judge leniency design extends the evidence to patients’ financial lives. Among nearly
30,000 patients linked to consumer credit records, where the average score of 591 is subprime,
assignment to an ED physician with a 5 pp higher propensity to initiate buprenorphine
raises credit scores by about 5.5 points and increases the probability of crossing into “good”
standing (a score above 670) by 4 pp from a 17% baseline. The improvement is concentrated
in fewer delinquencies and collections, and patients also gain available credit. For scale,
the 5.5 point reduced form effect is of the same order as the 2.4-point gain from a 7 pp
increase in insurance coverage under the Massachusetts reform (Mazumder and Miller, 2016).
Instrumenting buprenorphine receipt with physician propensity yields an estimated 135-point
increase in credit scores (95% confidence interval roughly 18 to 253), a large effect for the
high-risk patients physician assignment moves into treatment. Because veterans receive
nearly free care, relief from medical bills is an unlikely channel; the gains point to a broader
restoration of routine financial functioning.
2
These economic improvements accompany substantial estimated survival gains. The same
five-point increase in clinician adoption reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 pp,
a 23% reduction in a population where nearly one in six overdose survivors otherwise dies
within two years. An imprecise cause-of-death decomposition suggests reductions in both
drug-related and other deaths, with the latter accounting for most of the estimated decline,
and other health measures move the same way: depression (PHQ-9) scores fall 11%, with no
detectable increase in emergency visits or repeat overdoses. The physician-assignment design
provides additional evidence: assignment to a higher-propensity physician within the same
facility and quarter reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 0.6 pp from a 9% baseline
and raises engagement with care. Instrumenting receipt with physician propensity yields a
13 pp reduction for patients whose treatment physician assignment shifts. That estimate
applies to a high-risk group: these marginal patients would face two-year mortality of roughly
17% without buprenorphine. Both mortality estimates are imprecise, significant at the 10%
level, but stable across specifications. The two designs rest on different assumptions, so their
agreement does not depend on any single one.
Beyond these main results, we ask when the gains arise, for whom, and at what cost.
Treatment uptake and engagement with care respond within a month of the overdose, while
the survival and employment program responses accumulate over the following two years.
This sequence is consistent with treatment engagement preceding economic re-engagement.
Across patients, subgroup estimates suggest the largest survival gains for those in poor
physical health and the largest increases in engagement with care for those with serious
mental illness, suggesting that medication is most life-saving where physical risk is highest
and most valuable as a gateway to care where psychiatric illness is present. Buprenorphine
use rises with little net displacement of methadone, the other main medication for OUD, so
the expansion adds to medication treatment rather than reshuffling it. Finally, at a value
of $300,000 per statistical life-year, our point estimates imply that survival benefits alone
exceed the added medical spending over three years in the VA.
This paper contributes to the literature on the economic value of medical innovation.
Foundational work quantifies the welfare gains from improvements in health and longevity
(Murphy and Topel, 2006; Cutler and McClellan, 2001), while studies of specific technologies
document benefits beyond clinical outcomes, including labor market effects of pain medication,
antidepressant advertising, and radiotherapy (Garthwaite, 2012; Shapiro, 2022; Daysal et al.,
2025). Research on technology diffusion links the adoption of effective treatments to improve-
3
ments in patient survival and healthcare productivity (Skinner and Staiger, 2015). Related
work documents the financial costs of health shocks (Dobkin et al., 2018) and the protection
provided by health insurance (Hu et al., 2018; Mazumder and Miller, 2016; Miller et al., 2021).
We show that medical treatment can contribute to economic recovery from addiction: greater
access to buprenorphine improves financial health as well as survival. We separately identify
the effects of expanding prescribing capacity and of receiving buprenorphine, assessing both
the returns to wider adoption of a medical innovation in routine care and the benefits to
patients who receive the medication.
We also contribute to the literature on substance use disorder (SUD) treatment by
identifying the effects of medication on economic recovery and survival.1 Studies of treatment-
facility openings and closings document effects on drug-related mortality, emergency visits,
and crime (Swensen, 2015; Bullinger, Wang and Feder, 2022; Corredor-Waldron and Currie,
2022; Bondurant, Lindo and Swensen, 2018). The closest studies of expanded access to
buprenorphine find that greater prescriber availability shifts patients toward medication-
based treatment (Barrette, Dafny and Shen, 2023) and that expanded prescribing authority
reduces population opioid mortality (Gui, 2025). We extend this evidence in two ways.
On economic outcomes, we show that treatment improves patients’ financial health and
participation in employment programs.2 On mortality, we identify the effect of receiving
buprenorphine on patients’ all-cause mortality, rather than the population effect of expanded
access.3 We exploit quasi-random assignment to emergency physicians within the same facility
and quarter, accounting for shared changes in facility care that could confound estimates
based on facility adoption.
The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 provides background on
buprenorphine and its regulatory context. Section 3 describes the data, sample, and outcomes
we use. Section 4 outlines our two complementary empirical strategies. Section 5 presents
the main results and robustness checks. Section 6 examines dynamics, heterogeneity, and
mechanisms; Section 7 turns to a cost-benefit calculation and aggregate counterfactuals.
1The broader economics literature on the opioid crisis (reviewed by Maclean et al., 2022) examines the
epidemic’s origins (e.g., Alpert et al., 2022; Schnell, 2026; Finkelstein, Gentzkow and Li, 2025; Eichmeyer and
Zhang, 2022, 2023; Janssen and Zhang, 2023), evaluates supply-side interventions (e.g., Evans, Lieber and
Power, 2019; Buchmueller and Carey, 2018; Soliman, 2025), and documents its economic and intergenerational
costs (Laird and Nielsen, 2016; Currie, Jin and Schnell, 2019; Buckles, Evans and Lieber, 2023).
2Evidence on patients’ economic outcomes includes education and employment following residential SUD
treatment for adolescents (Kim, 2023) and employment following changes in waiting times for outpatient
cannabis treatment (Williams, Bretteville-Jensen and Rose, 2026).
3Also related is work that examines the mortality effects of delays in mental health care among VA
patients (Costantini, 2025).
4
Finally, Section 8 concludes.
2 Background: Buprenorphine
Buprenorphine is a semi-synthetic opioid first approved by the U.S. FDA in 2002 for the
maintenance treatment of opioid use disorder. A single daily dose suppresses withdrawal
and blocks the reinforcing effects of subsequent opioid use (Volkow and Blanco, 2020), and
these properties place it at the center of the World Health Organization’s and the Substance
Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s (SAMHSA) treatment guidelines (World
Health Organization, 2009; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration,
2021). Unlike methadone, the other widely used medication for OUD, buprenorphine can be
prescribed in office-based settings and dispensed in take-home supplies, sparing most patients
the supervised dosing required at federally regulated opioid treatment programs and allowing
treatment to scale far beyond specialized clinic capacity (Volkow and Blanco, 2020; Blanco
and Volkow, 2019).4 Yet most U.S. patients with OUD receive no treatment at all, and only
about a third of those who do receive medication (Williams et al., 2018).
Prescribing and administering buprenorphine. For most of our study period, prescribing
buprenorphine for OUD outside certified opioid treatment programs required a federal “X-
waiver,” which entailed eight hours of training for physicians (24 for nurse practitioners and
physician assistants) and capped the number of patients a clinician could treat (SAMHSA,
2021). Adoption was slow and highly uneven: beyond the training cost, many clinicians
were reluctant to treat addiction at all, citing stigma, lack of institutional support, and
unfamiliarity with the medication (Blanco and Volkow, 2019). Within the VA, the share of
clinicians who had begun prescribing buprenorphine rose at different times across facilities
over two decades. This staggered, facility-level variation is the basis of our first research
design.5
4Randomized trials establish buprenorphine’s efficacy for treatment retention and reduced illicit opioid
use, but evidence on mortality rests on few trials and very few deaths (Mattick et al., 2014). Observational
studies associate buprenorphine with better health outcomes (e.g., Weiner et al., 2024; Larochelle et al., 2018).
Evidence from other delivery settings links buprenorphine provided during incarceration to lower post-release
recidivism (Evans, Wilson and Friedmann, 2022) and ambulance-based initiation after an overdose to greater
short-term treatment engagement (Carroll et al., 2023).
5The training requirement was relaxed in April 2021 for eligible clinicians treating up to 30 patients,
and the waiver was eliminated in January 2023; studies of both changes find little effect on buprenorphine
treatment (Christine et al., 2024; Chua et al., 2024). These findings are not at odds with our study: we
capture the effect of clinicians’ actual adoption of prescribing, whereas removing a regulatory barrier may
leave other obstacles to adoption in place.
5
Alongside the waiver regime, federal regulation provided a narrower pathway for un-
waivered clinicians, known as the “3-day rule”: any DEA-registered practitioner could
administer (but not prescribe) one day’s dose of buprenorphine to a patient in acute with-
drawal, repeated for up to 72 hours, to stabilize the patient while arranging referral to
formal treatment (U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, 2020). The rule matters most
in emergency departments, where patients in withdrawal frequently present. Whether a
given ED physician uses this authority, however, is largely a matter of individual practice
style: initiation rates vary widely and persistently across physicians working in the same
department.
These two rules generate the variation behind our two empirical strategies. In the facility
adoption difference-in-differences design, the treatment variable is the share of a facility’s
non-ED clinicians who have prescribed or administered buprenorphine, the clinicians able to
provide sustained outpatient treatment; we exclude ED providers, whose 3-day-rule authority
requires no waiver and does not reflect longer term prescribing capacity. The ED physician
propensity design exploits persistent differences across ED physicians in their tendency to
initiate buprenorphine, which the emergency exception makes possible: because any ED
physician can administer it to a patient in withdrawal without a waiver, initiation is a matter
of individual practice style, and the effectively random assignment of unplanned ED arrivals
to physicians on shift turns that variation into quasi-experimental variation in receipt of the
medication at the emergency visit.
3 Data
We analyze data from 2003 through 2025 from the Veterans Health Administration (VA), the
largest integrated healthcare system in the United States, which provides care to more than
9 million eligible veterans through 170 medical centers and over 1,300 outpatient facilities.6
Because eligibility is stable and untied to employment, we observe complete (within-VA)
clinical and program histories, with virtually no insurance-related attrition, among the more
than 140,000 veterans with OUD we study.
Our data cover every healthcare encounter delivered within the VA system (outpatient vis-
its, inpatient admissions, and pharmacy dispensing) with structured diagnosis and procedure
codes, provider and facility identifiers, and time-stamped clinical events. We additionally
6Eligibility includes prior active-duty service, discharge under conditions other than dishonorable, and
either income-based qualification or a service-connected disability.
6
observe rich clinical metrics that are rarely available in claims data, such as structured mental
health assessments (e.g., PHQ-9 depression scores). Beyond medical care, the data link to
VA-administered social programs, including vocational rehabilitation, employment assistance,
and disability compensation, allowing us to track economic and psychosocial outcomes within
the same administrative universe.
To capture care veterans receive outside the VA system, we also link to Medicare Parts A,
B, and D claims (2014–2019), Medicaid claims (2014–2015), and VA-reimbursed community
care records. The latter includes all emergency services delivered at non-VA facilities, which is
particularly important for opioid-related health crises. Finally, we observe complete mortality
data from the CDC National Death Index Plus, including date and cause of death, ensuring
that long-run health outcomes are measured without loss to follow-up.
To measure patients’ financial health, we additionally link veterans to consumer credit
records from TransUnion, one of the three major U.S. credit bureaus. The linkage is built
from a random sample of just over 300,000 veterans with an emergency department visit
between 2014 and 2018, which we provided to TransUnion for matching based on veterans’
social security numbers; approximately 93% of these veterans have at least one credit report
record. For each such veteran, we observe a quarterly panel of credit report information
for the two years before and the two years after the ED visit, including individual-level
data on credit scores and on the balances, credit limits, delinquencies, and third-party
collections reported across open accounts. These records provide a market-based, objectively
reported summary of financial stability that complements the VA’s administrative measures
of economic engagement.
3.1 Sample
In our primary empirical research design, which exploits facility and time variation in provider
buprenorphine adoption rates, we include all VA patients who experience a VA ED visit for an
opioid overdose in the years 2004–2022. We restrict the sample to the patient’s first qualifying
ED opioid overdose event. The rationale for selecting overdose events is twofold. First,
overdoses serve as a highly objective indicator of severe opioid use disorder, increasing the
likelihood these individuals are clinically appropriate candidates for initiating buprenorphine
treatment. Second, by relying on overdose rather than a previous diagnosis of OUD, we avoid
endogenous selection biases related to variation across facilities and time in OUD diagnosis
practices. One might worry that facility-time variation in buprenorphine adoption could itself
7
influence which patients present with an overdose; we find no evidence of such compositional
selection (Section 5.3).
Our second strategy uses all VA patients with an ED visit between 2004 and 2022
and an OUD diagnosis in the prior year, again keeping each patient’s first qualifying visit.
Conditioning on a prior diagnosis rather than an overdose is possible here because the design
compares patients assigned to different physicians within a facility and quarter, so facility-level
variation in diagnosis practice cannot confound it, and it yields a sample nearly twenty times
larger, which the IV analysis needs.
Our analysis of financial outcomes applies this second strategy to the TransUnion-linked
subsample: veterans with an ED visit between 2014 and 2018, again keeping each patient’s
first qualifying visit and requiring a prior-year OUD diagnosis. Among the 82,889 patients
meeting these criteria, 35.7% have an observed credit score and enter the financial outcomes
sample.7
In all samples, we drop terminal cancer and end-of-life geriatric patients, as well as
patients who die within seven days of the ED encount

is approximately 43% of its month-24 value, while the increase in monthly vocational

Two conclusions follow. First, the response to the crisis moment is not transient. Medica-
tion use and engagement with care remain elevated two years after the overdose, though at
a fraction of their initial level. Thus, the adherence concern raised in the introduction is a
matter of degree: engagement attenuates but does not disappear. Second, the sequence is
consistent with treatment engagement facilitating economic re-engagement, with treatment
responding first and survival and employment-program gains following over the subsequent
two years.
The timing also matters for valuation. The costs of expanded adoption arrive mostly
in the first year while the survival benefits build over time, which is why the cost-benefit
calculation in Section 7.1 turns positive only in the third year.
6.2 Heterogeneity
Medications for OUD may not translate into broad and sustained life improvements for
everyone. Even if adherence is achieved, health gains may not automatically spill over into
economic or psychosocial domains, especially for patients burdened by severe co-morbidities
or serious mental illness. To probe these possibilities, we examine whether the effects of
buprenorphine access differ systematically across patient subgroups defined by their prior
health status and treatment history.
We consider four natural margins of heterogeneity, each intended to capture a distinct
dimension of baseline patient risk. First, we split patients by whether their number of prior
Elixhauser comorbidities is above or below the median, using this as a summary measure of
their overall physical health. Second, we separate patients by the presence or absence of a
serious mental illness diagnosis (such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or major depressive
disorder) in the prior year, to test whether psychiatric conditions influence patients’ ability
to benefit. Third, we distinguish between patients who did or did not receive buprenorphine
treatment in the year prior to their overdose, using this as a proxy for OUD severity and
prior engagement with treatment. Fourth, we split patients by whether they are of working
age. For each subgroup, we re-estimate our facility-level adoption design, and present the
results in Figure 6.
For medically sick patients, the return to medication appears to be survival rather than
economic re-engagement. Patients with above-median Elixhauser scores have larger estimated
25
survival gains from buprenorphine access but smaller estimated increases in vocational
rehabilitation participation than healthier patients, though the difference in mortality effects
is imprecisely estimated (interaction p-value 0.11). The smaller economic response is likely
a matter of age: patients with more comorbidities are also older, and for many of them
returning to work is no longer realistic, which is what the age split below shows.
For patients with serious mental illness, medication appears to work mainly as a gateway
to care. Their estimated increases in engagement with medical care are the largest of any
group: outpatient visits and both mental and physical health encounters rise more sharply
once buprenorphine is available. Their estimated survival improvement is smaller than for
patients without serious mental illness, plausibly because a larger share of their baseline
mortality risk runs through causes, such as suicide and chronic disease, that medication for
OUD addresses only indirectly.
Prior buprenorphine users, patients who had already initiated treatment at some point
before their overdose, respond strongly across every margin. They show higher gains in
outpatient engagement, more pronounced survival benefits, and a larger boost in vocational
rehabilitation enrollment, despite a smaller increase in buprenorphine uptake itself (since
many were already on the medication). Because prior users are, by construction, patients
already engaged with treatment, this pattern admits two readings: larger treatment effects for
patients already connected to care, or favorable selection into prior use; we do not distinguish
them here. This group’s uptake response is smallest while its outcome responses are largest,
suggesting a large effect per unit of induced treatment.
Finally, the age split sharpens the interpretation of the economic effects and helps
disentangle the comorbidity results above, since worse physical health and older age are
strongly correlated in our sample. The vocational rehabilitation response is concentrated
largely among patients of prime working age (we split at 55, the upper bound of the standard
25–54 prime working age definition), at 1.8 pp versus 0.7 pp for patients 55 and older (panel (d)
of Figure 6), though the difference between age groups is not statistically distinguishable. The
pattern is consistent with enrollment in employment programs reflecting genuine movement
toward work among those for whom work is a feasible margin, rather than an artifact
of program reclassification. Survival gains, by contrast, are larger among older patients,
indicating that the life-saving and economic margins of buprenorphine operate on partially
distinct subpopulations.
These findings speak to the motivating question of whether and for whom medical
26
innovation translates into real-world improvements. Taken together, the heterogeneity results
show that buprenorphine’s benefits are not evenly distributed. They appear most life-saving
for those in poor physical health, largest for care engagement among those with serious
mental illness, most broad-based for those who had prior exposure to treatment, and, on the
economic margin, operative chiefly among those of working age.
6.3 Substitution from Methadone
Buprenorphine and methadone are the two most widely used evidence-based, first-line
treatments for opioid use disorder. It is therefore natural to ask whether expanding access
to one therapy simply displaces patients from the other; answering this question clarifies
whether the benefits we estimate reflect a reallocation of existing patients across medications
or extensive margin responses of engaging new patients in MOUD treatment. To do so,
we re-estimate our baseline facility adoption empirical design for the outcome of a patient
receiving methadone treatment in a given month.
The estimated effect on methadone use is 0.6 pp and statistically indistinguishable from
zero (Table A.9). The 95% confidence interval excludes a net decline larger than approximately
0.4 pp, less than a tenth of the 4.7 pp increase in buprenorphine use. Thus, substitution from
methadone can account for at most a small share of the gain in buprenorphine treatment.
Similarly, assignment to an ED physician with a higher buprenorphine prescribing propensity
has no detectable effect on emergency methadone treatment or referral to an opioid treatment
program at the index visit (Table C.1). The improvements we document therefore come
largely from drawing new patients onto evidence-based medication rather than reshuffling
existing patients across therapies.
7 Policy Implications
7.1 Cost-Benefit Analysis
We conduct a cost-benefit calculation that compares the value of the estimated survival
gains with the medical and medication costs of expanding buprenorphine prescribing. We
consider the same five-point increase in the caseload-weighted share of clinicians with prior
buprenorphine prescribing experience, approximately the gap between facilities at the 10th
and 90th percentiles in 2018. We measure the gains in life-years, the extra time that patients
live within each period, and put a dollar value on each life-year. We use $300,000 per
27
statistical life-year as our central benchmark, informed by the life-year valuations in Murphy
and Topel (2006).17 This asks whether survival alone can justify the extra spending, before
placing any value on improvements in patients’ wellbeing or economic circumstances. All
amounts are averages over all overdose patients in the sample. They add up costs or benefits
over the first one, two, or three years after the overdose.
For a 5 pp increase in facility prescribing adoption, the estimated additional cost over three
years is $8,087 per overdose patient: $7,572 in medical spending and $515 in buprenorphine.
The estimated survival gain is 0.0347 life-years per patient, worth approximately $10,400 at
the $300,000 valuation. The resulting net benefit is approximately $2,300 per patient.18 The
balance is less favorable over shorter horizons: most added costs arise in the first year, while
survival benefits accumulate over time, leaving net benefits negative after one and two years.
Table 6 reports the results for each time horizon.
The conclusion depends on the value assigned to an additional year of life. Over three
years, benefits and costs break even at approximately $233,000 per life-year. At $200,000,
costs exceed benefits by $1,148 per patient; at $400,000, benefits exceed costs by $5,792.
Discounting future costs and benefits at 3% annually reduces the net benefit at the $300,000
valuation to approximately $1,900.
For perspective, our estimated cost of $233,000 per life-year gained is similar in magnitude
to the approximately $220,000 in direct budgetary costs per life-year gained from Medicaid
expansions estimated by Wyse and Meyer (2025), expressed in 2024 dollars.19 Their calculation
includes projected gains over patients’ remaining lifetimes, while ours counts only life-years
gained within three years of the overdose. The comparison therefore provides a benchmark
for scale rather than a ranking of the interventions.
The positive balance is subject to uncertainty in the estimated survival gains and spending;
we do not report a confidence interval for net benefits. For simplicity and clarity, the
calculation also omits some costs and benefits. Costs exclude the expense of increasing
adoption itself, such as clinician training. At the central valuation, our point estimates
leave approximately $2,300 per overdose patient to cover such implementation costs within
the three-year calculation. Benefits exclude survival gains beyond the three-year horizon.

7.2 Aggregate Counterfactuals
We use the above mentioned cost and benefit estimates to illustrate what wider buprenorphine
adoption could mean for patients who have overdosed.20 We first consider one future year of
overdose patients in the VA, taking a cohort of 500 patients.21 If the estimated per-patient
effects and costs apply to this cohort, a 5 pp increase in facility prescribing adoption would
imply approximately 19 fewer deaths over the following two years and $1.2 million in net
benefits over three years, valuing each additional life-year at $300,000 (Table D.1).
We also ask what the same expansion could have achieved for the overdose patients
treated over our study period. Across the 7,517 patients in our facility-adoption sample, a
5 pp increase in prescribing adoption implies approximately 278 fewer deaths within two
years and 261 life-years gained over three years. At $300,000 per life-year, the three-year
survival benefits amount to $78.2 million, compared with $60.8 million in added medical and
buprenorphine costs.
These calculations illustrate the stakes of wider adoption: under our central assumptions,
bringing an existing medication to more patients could yield substantial survival gains whose
value exceeds the additional medical spending.
8 Conclusion
Medical treatment can contribute to economic recovery from addiction. Our evidence from
the Veterans Health Administration shows that expanding access to buprenorphine produces
benefits in routine care. A 5 pp increase in prescribing adoption raises treatment uptake and
engagement with care and reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 23% in a population
where one in six patients otherwise dies. The benefits extend beyond health: participation
in employment programs rises, and the physician-assignment design provides evidence of
improvedfinancialhealth. Thesefindingsshowthatthedisadvantagesaccompanyingaddiction
need not prevent economic gains from treatment. At a value of $300,000 per statistical
life-year, our point estimates imply that survival benefits alone exceed the added medical
spending over three years.

The benefits develop over time. Treatment use and engagement with care rise promptly,
while gains in survival and employment-program participation emerge more gradually. This
pattern is consistent with treatment engagement supporting economic recovery. Whether
complementary social and employment supports can strengthen that recovery remains an
important question. Our findings also highlight the role of adoption in realizing the value of
medical innovation. Studies of relaxed training requirements and X-waiver elimination find
limited growth in the number of patients receiving treatment (Christine et al., 2024; Chua
et al., 2024); our estimates show the potential gains when expanded prescribing capacity
brings patients into care. Policies that help clinicians incorporate buprenorphine into routine
practice, through training, institutional support, and reimbursement, may therefore be
important complements to regulatory reform.
Several caveats apply. The estimates come from an older, predominantly male veteran
population treated in an integrated health system; our economic measures include credit
records and program participation, but not observed employment or earnings; and the
physician-design estimates apply to patients whose treatment physician assignment shifts,
who are at higher risk than the average patient with OUD. The estimates also capture
only effects on the patient. Treatment may generate additional benefits for spouses and
intergenerational impacts through children and other family members. Finally, the size of
the estimated gains makes clinician adoption itself an important object of study: identifying
which barriers matter most, and which policies actually increase prescribing, is the next step
in converting clinical efficacy into recovery from one of the deadliest public health crises in
U.S. history.
